title: Latency ephemeral capture playbook — cohort snapshot & per-stage profiler
content:
Purpose:
This is a short, practical playbook for capturing high-resolution, short-duration trace snapshots ("ephemeral captures") when we see: p99 regressions, microburst behavior, or unexplained tail events. The goal is to produce compact, reproducible per-stage breakdowns (tokenize, batch-wait, KV-fetch, model-forward, emit/egress, network) with p50/p95/p99 numbers and a contextual cohort filter so follow-up investigations can be narrow and actionable.

Why ephemeral captures?
- Continuous full-detail tracing at production QPS is expensive and noisy.
- Ephemeral captures let us: trigger on a tail condition, collect richer per-token and stage timings for a focused period (~30s–2m), and then auto-expire.
- The playbook here standardizes trigger rules, capture config, and a minimal analysis checklist so different engineers generate comparable artifacts.

When to use this playbook (trigger examples):
- Route p99 > 900ms for more than 30s (observed on route /v1/generate)
- Sudden jump in batch-wait variance (p95 batch-wait > 40ms)
- Large increase in KV-miss ratio coincident with tail events

Capture configuration (recommended defaults):
- Window: 60s rolling snap (configurable 30s–120s)
- Trigger: p99(route) > 900ms OR sudden spike in p95 batch-wait relative to 5m baseline (>3x)
- Sampling mode: full-trace for all requests that hit p95+ during window; 1% background sampling for p50 baseline
- Metadata to record: route, model-version, instance-type, seq-len, batch-size, client-region, token-count, kv-hit/miss flags, cold-start flag
- Max traces: 200 per window (cull oldest if exceeded)

Data hygiene notes:
- Strip PII before long-term storage. Ephemeral captures are allowed to contain prompts for debugging but must be redacted before saving to long-term artifact store.
- Keep ephemeral store TTL = 24h; if attached to a Jira, export sanitized snapshot as .json and place link in ticket.

Analysis checklist (what to compute from each capture):
1) Aggregate p50/p95/p99 for end-to-end response time (ms) for the capture cohort.
2) Per-stage quantiles (tokenize, prebatch, batch-wait, kv-fetch, model-forward, emit, network) with p50/p95/p99.
3) Sequence-length stratification: split cohort into short (<=64), mid (65–256), long (>256) and report quantiles per stratum.
4) Batch-size correlation: correlate batch-size at request time with end-to-end latency (scatter + bucketed quantiles).
5) KV-hit vs KV-miss split for model-forward timing and batch-wait.
6) Cold-starts flagged and excluded from comparison baseline unless investigating cold path.

Example snapshot (realistic numbers from recent capture on route /v1/chat):
- Cohort: 120 traces, window=60s, model=rwd-3b-quant, instances=g5-4x
- End-to-end (ms): p50=82, p95=430, p99=1020

Per-stage breakdown (ms, quantiles):
- Tokenize: p50=2, p95=6, p99=12
- Prebatch (parsing + routing): p50=5, p95=20, p99=45
- Batch-wait: p50=10, p95=160, p99=520
- KV-fetch (cache lookup + network hop): p50=6, p95=18, p99=60
- Model-forward (first token latency + streaming): p50=35, p95=110, p99=250
- Emit/egress (serialize + flush): p50=4, p95=8, p99=20
- Network RTT (client-facing): p50=10, p95=45, p99=120

Interpretation notes on the example:
- The dominant contributor at p99 is batch-wait (520ms). Model-forward is elevated but not the p99 driver.
- High p95 for batch-wait suggests intermittent queuing caused by a small number of large batches or contention on the async-batcher.
- KV-fetch p99=60ms is non-trivial but not the main tail contributor here.

Quick hypotheses to validate (ordered):
H1: A handful of unusually large sequence-length requests caused long batch assembly times -> reproduce by replaying long-seqlen traces against batcher simulator.
H2: Async-batcher had eviction/backpressure during the window -> check batcher queue depth/traces around capture window and correlate with instance GC/IO metrics.
H3: One or two instances had degraded kernel scheduling (noisy neighbor) -> map traces to instance id and compare host-level CPU steal, io-wait, and temperature events.

Validation steps (what I did in the capture above):
- Replayed top-10 p99 traces in local microbench harness; confirmed that when submitted in isolation they complete ~120–180ms (so model-forward alone doesn't explain p99).
- Extracted batch assembly timeline from traces: found 6 traces where request waited >400ms for batch to fill; batch sizes were 16–32 while median is 6–8.
- Cross-checked platform metrics: during window there was a small spike in ingress (QPS +18%) and one autoscale event that briefly increased queueing while warm-up completed.

Remediation options (short list):
- Short-term: add a fallback cap on batch-wait for p99-critical routes (e.g., max batch-wait 120ms -> force partial dispatch) and monitor quality regression.
- Mid-term: tune adaptive-batcher policy to avoid building few very large batches (prefer more uniform batch-size bins).
- Long-term: implement per-route burst tanks or offer a premium low-latency route with stricter batching/capacity.

Reporting template (what to paste into Jira):
- Snapshot ID, time window, route, model-version, instance-type
- Cohort counts and seq-len distribution
- End-to-end p50/p95/p99 + per-stage p50/p95/p99 table (text)
- Short diagnosis summary + top hypothesis + recommended immediate mitigation
- Link to sanitized ephemeral capture export (or attach .json)

Open questions / TODOs:
- (Samira) Build an automated check that flags "batch-size variance" > 3x in capture window (INF ticket?)
- (Marcus) Confirm whether autoscaler warm-up is contributing routinely; correlate with scale events (Eleanor to help fetch logs).
- (Eleanor) Add small wrapper to redaction pipeline so ephemeral captures attached to Jira are auto-sanitized before upload.

Appendix: small notes on measurement pitfalls
- Don’t double-count time that overlaps stages (e.g., model-forward streaming + emit flush); define stage boundaries consistently in capture agent.
- Account for instrumentation overhead (sampling/trace header adds ~1–3ms). Run a baseline capture with instrumentation but no load to calibrate.
- When comparing model-versions, lock hardware type and instance configuration; small CPU differences on host can bias p95/p99.

If you use this playbook, paste the capture ID to the ticket and tag #latency-ephemeral. If the capture shows persistent p99 drivers we should convert the ephemeral snapshot to a longer retention artifact and schedule a deeper postmortem.

End of playbook — quick note: the capture above is saved as ephemeral:cap-20250110-18-42 (will expire +24h); sanitized export uploaded to JIRA-INF-457 as attachment.
